A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same multiplication-free channel-wise parallel spiking neuron and training accelerator, despite the changed title and format. Their text, equations, figures, tables, and complete appendices support comparison.

before.justification: v1 reports original classification results, neuron-order and dilation ablations, GPU training timings, and a training-collapse analysis in the main text and appendices.

after.justification: v2 retains original classification and ablation results, reports SHD results across three seeds, and adds inference-memory comparisons and further GPU training timings.

M1.justification: The reported acceleration candidate set drops Time-first + Reshape + Conv2d, explicitly included in v1 Section 4.3 but absent from v2's corresponding main-text and Appendix A lists. The neuronal dynamics, power-of-two quantization, straight-through estimator, batch-normalization fusion, and autoselect pseudocode otherwise remain unchanged.

E1.justification: Both versions evaluate SHD, sequential CIFAR10/CIFAR100, pixel CIFAR10, and DVS-Lip, with CIFAR100 also used for timing. The additional hardware, batch-size, memory, and energy evaluations retain this dataset and task coverage.

E2.justification: The training-speed comparison removes the naive time-last implementation shown in v1 Figure 7 and Table 7. v2 Figure 6 retains the time-first implementation under the name Vanilla, alongside PSN/sliding PSN and autoselect. Comparator membership in the classification tables is unchanged.

E3.justification: Appendix E changes SHD from no augmentation to spatial jitter, noise, and event dropping. Its batch size changes from 256 to 128, with weight/delay learning rates reduced from 0.001/0.1 to 0.0005/0.05. v2 also adds H20 timing at batch size 128, A100 timing at sizes 32 and 64, and inference-memory and operation-based energy evaluation protocols. These substantially expand settings and revise the SHD protocol.

E4.justification: v2 adds analyses of inference memory, neuronal versus synaptic energy, autoselect overhead, and timing sensitivity to GPU and batch size in Sections 5.3–5.5 and Appendices F–G. The CIFAR order/dilation ablations and DVS-Lip gradient-collapse analysis are retained. SHD results at orders 4 and 8 are no longer reported.

E5.justification: v2 first reports SHD uncertainty for the proposed method, 95.50 ± 0.36% across seeds 0, 1, and 2, and adds uncertainty to the Hammouamri comparator. Section 4.3 also newly specifies 2m+1 timing executions with the last m averaged. These are reporting additions; v1 does not establish earlier run counts, and most accuracy results still lack uncertainty.

E6.justification: New results include 547 versus 2635 MB inference memory for ours at k=4 versus sliding PSN at k=32, and estimated energy of 10.66 versus 91.62 microjoules for ours versus PSN. Additional GPU/batch timings and autoselect overheads are reported. SHD's 95.31/95.62/95.71% at k=2/4/8 is replaced by 95.50 ± 0.36% at k=2 under revised settings, not a directly comparable gain or loss. Hammouamri's score changes from 95.10 to 95.07 ± 0.24%. Sequential CIFAR, DVS-Lip, and the tabulated CIFAR ablation accuracies remain unchanged.

T1.justification: v2 adds method-specific parameter and operation counts in Table 1 and analytical energy expressions in Appendix F/Table 9. These include the k=T expression 0.515T²+1.415T for the proposed neuron versus 4.6T²+0.9T for PSN. This is a limited new cost derivation; the existing neuronal and training equations are retained.

C1.justification: Introduction contribution 1 explicitly adds significantly reduced inference memory to the earlier unchanged-FLOPs claim. The central contributions concerning channel-wise dynamics, dilations, multiplication-free inference, temporal learning, and automatic acceleration remain substantively the same.

C2.justification: New Sections 5.4–5.5 explain memory savings through shorter stored input histories and attribute PSN's dominant neuronal energy cost to dense multiplication. They qualify energy estimation by using fixed-point shift energy as an approximation for floating-point implementation. Appendix H largely repeats v1's existing explanation of slower training rather than introducing a new limitation.

D1.justification: v2 adds a GitHub code-access link and documents floating-point exponent arithmetic, second-epoch steady-state timing, and the operation costs and test-set firing rates used for energy estimation. Most architecture specifications, batch-normalization fusion details, Triton pseudocode, and training documentation were already present in v1.

R1.justification: v2 adds DenseShift and ShiftAddNAS citations supporting floating-point implementation and energy accounting. Removing the Spiking Deep Learning subsection also removes its Cao et al., Fast-SNN, and Xception references. The positioning relative to existing spiking neuron models remains largely unchanged.

P1.justification: v2 retitles the paper, edits introductory and preliminary explanations, removes the Spiking Deep Learning background subsection, and rewrites Section 4.3 around data layouts while moving implementation descriptions into Appendix A. These are localized editorial and organizational changes; most prose and the overall argument remain recognizable.

P2.justification: The paper changes from a two-column to a single-column layout. v1's separate quantization figures are merged into v2 Figure 3, the memory-layout diagram gains a legend, and the timing chart is redesigned with numerical labels and fewer comparator groups. New parameter, memory, energy, and hardware-timing tables substantially expand the visual presentation.

improvement.justification: v2 strengthens v1's hardware-efficiency argument with explicit memory comparisons, network-level energy accounting, and timing checks across GPUs and batch sizes. SHD uncertainty reporting, clearer timing documentation, and a code-access link also improve transparency. The gains are useful but bounded: energy remains an assumption-based estimate rather than measured hardware consumption, and the timing comparison loses the time-last control.
